citation: (1) Warm, J.S., Parasuraman, R., & Matthews, G. (2008). Vigilance requires hard mental work and is stressful. Human Factors, 50(3), 433-441. PMID 18689050; DOI 10.1177/0018720808320710. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18689050/ (2) Wohleber, R.W., Matthews, G., Lin, J., Szalma, J.L., Calhoun, G.L., Funke, G.J., Chiu, C.-Y.P., & Ruff, H.A. (2019). Vigilance and Automation Dependence in Operation of Multiple Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS): A Simulation Study. Human Factors, 61(3), 488-505. DOI 10.1177/0018720818799468. https://sciences.ucf.edu/psychology/perl/wp-content/uploads/sites/29/2019/08/Wohleber-et-al.-Vigilance-and-Automation.pdf
source_tier: Peer-reviewed (both, Human Factors). Warm et al. is a narrative review; Wohleber et al. is an experimental simulation study.
access_status: Warm, Parasuraman & Matthews 2008: ABSTRACT ONLY (structured abstract retrieved from PubMed via NCBI efetch; the SAGE page returned 403 and full text was not opened). Wohleber et al. 2019: FULLY READ (full article PDF, author-hosted at UCF, text extracted and read). Note: Wohleber et al. was a 2018 online / May 2019 print article, Human Factors 61(3), a special issue in remembrance of Joel Warm.
sponsor_and_incentive: Wohleber et al.: sponsored by AFOSR (grants A955013-1-0016 and 13RH05COR); authors include Air Force Research Laboratory staff; no product sold. Warm et al. 2008: funding not stated in the abstract [uncertain]; no commercial incentive evident.
exact_quotes: Warm et al. 2008 (PubMed abstract, BACKGROUND): "Vigilance tasks have typically been viewed as undemanding assignments requiring little mental effort. The vigilance decrement function has also been considered to result from a decline in arousal brought about by understimulation." | (RESULTS): "Subjective reports also show that the workload of vigilance is high and sensitive to factors that increase processing demands." | (RESULTS): "physiological and subjective reports confirm that vigilance tasks reduce task engagement and increase distress and that these changes rise with increased task difficulty." | (CONCLUSIONS): "Converging evidence using behavioral, neural, and subjective measures shows that vigilance requires hard mental work and is stressful." | (APPLICATION): "This research applies to most human-machine systems that require human monitoring, particularly those involving automated subsystems." || Wohleber et al. 2019 (abstract): "Performance accuracy on the more demanding surveillance task showed a vigilance decrement, especially when automation reliability was low. Dependence on automation on this task declined over time. State but not trait factors predicted performance. High distress was associated with poorer performance in more demanding task conditions." | (Intro, p.490): "automation that relegates the operator to a passive monitoring role could exacerbate vigilance decrement (Warm, Parasuraman, & Matthews, 2008)." | (Discussion): "However, the NASA-TLX workload of 35.8 was well below the scale midpoint of 50" | (Discussion): "The stability of distress across the trial was also unexpected" | (Discussion): "passive fatigue may be an operational issue even when operators are required to perform routine task activities, given sufficient task duration." | (Discussion): "over shorter durations, UAS surveillance tasks may be less vulnerable to decrement than laboratory studies would suggest." | (Conclusion): "The Warm et al. (1996) resource theory does not fully explain the effects observed"
date_and_recency: Warm et al.: 2008 (Human Factors 50(3)). Wohleber et al.: online 2018, print May 2019; data collected in a 2 hr simulated task session (4 hr test session) with UCF students; collection dates not stated in the text I read [uncertain].
key_claims: Warm et al. 2008 (review, per abstract): vigilance tasks were long assumed undemanding and the decrement attributed to understimulation/low arousal; converging behavioural, neural (transcranial Doppler) and subjective evidence instead supports an attentional resource theory in which vigilance is hard mental work and is stressful. Applies to human-machine systems requiring monitoring, particularly with automated subsystems. Wohleber et al. 2019: in a 2 hr multi-UAS simulation with low cognitive demands, accuracy on the more demanding surveillance task (WR) showed a vigilance decrement, worse with low automation reliability; reliance on automation fell over time; large loss of task engagement; distress (state, not personality traits) predicted poorer performance under demanding conditions. Authors say Warm's resource theory does not fully explain the pattern (workload was modest, distress did not rise).
headline_figures: Wohleber: N = 131 participants; 2 hr task (within a 4 hr session); performance scored per 15-min interval; NASA-TLX workload 35.8 (scale midpoint 50), i.e. low, not high; low-reliability condition WR accuracy "fairly stable for the first 45 min, declined progressively for the next hour, and recovered sharply in the final 15 min" (end effect); typical laboratory decrement happens in first 20-30 min. Comparison cited from another study (Matthews et al. 2014): distress rose by nearly 1 SD during a 1 hr map-display vigil. Warm et al. 2008: no numbers in the abstract.
sample_unit_and_population: Wohleber: 131 University of Central Florida undergraduate psychology students (50 women, 81 men, mean age 19.86, range 18-31), civilians, untrained, not software engineers; automation reliability manipulated between groups. Warm et al.: literature review of vigilance research, mostly laboratory participants; not software engineers.
observed_vs_stated: Mixed. Warm et al. synthesises behavioural performance, neural blood-flow (TCD) measures and subjective workload/stress reports. Wohleber: observed accuracy and automation-dependence behaviour plus self-reported state (Dundee Stress State Questionnaire, NASA-TLX).
what_makes_oversight_tiring: Warm et al. (abstract): sustained attention draws on limited attentional resources, so keeping watch is effortful; workload ratings are high and rise with processing demands; vigilance reduces task engagement and raises distress, more so as difficulty rises. Wohleber: automation that makes the operator a passive monitor may worsen the decrement; they also report passive fatigue (big engagement loss) even where workload was low.
consequence_for_quality: Wohleber: lower detection/discrimination accuracy on the harder task over time, stronger with unreliable automation; higher distress tied to worse accuracy in demanding conditions; operators increasingly under-used automation over time. Warm et al.: the performance decrement is linked to resource depletion (per abstract).
what_reduces_the_load: Wohleber (practical implications): workload mitigation, supporting operator motivation on long missions, interface design that raises the salience of automation recommendations plus training, possible diagnostic monitoring of stress and fatigue to drive adaptive automation. Authors note task variety/active involvement can counter the decrement (Parsons et al. 2007 eliminated it in a detection-action scenario; this is cited, not tested here). Warm et al. abstract gives no specific remedies beyond design of work environments and evaluating monitors (as quoted in Wohleber p.438 citation).
limitations_stated: Wohleber: "An obvious limitation is the use of untrained civilian participants rather than Air Force personnel"; a simulation "cannot fully capture operational conditions"; automation "limited in nature" with no test of transparency; variability in event frequency and reliability between blocks added noise; dependence metric does not show how participants reached decisions; operational stressors such as sleep and long hours not captured. Warm et al.: limitations not visible from the abstract.
counter_evidence: Wohleber itself cuts against a simple reading: workload was low (NASA-TLX 35.8), distress did not increase, decrement onset was delayed (not the usual 20-30 min), the easier task showed no sustained decrement, and the authors say real UAS tasks "may be less vulnerable to decrement than laboratory studies would suggest". It also cites critics of the resource account (Hancock 2013 attributes the decrement to boredom and loss of agency from display design; Thomson, Besner & Smilek 2016; Casner & Schooler 2015 on natural breaks), cited second-hand, not opened.
verification_status: Warm et al. 2008 title, conclusion, workload/stress/engagement statements: checked against the PubMed abstract actually opened; full-text details NOT verified [uncertain]. Wohleber et al. all figures and quotes above: checked against the full text actually opened. Claims about Hancock, Casner & Schooler, Parsons et al., Matthews 2014 are second-hand via Wohleber, not verified at source [uncertain].
usable_claim: A 2008 Human Factors review (Warm, Parasuraman and Matthews) concluded that converging behavioural, neural and subjective evidence shows vigilance 'requires hard mental work and is stressful', and that it applies to monitoring of automated systems. A 2019 Human Factors simulation (Wohleber et al., 131 students, 2 hr, multiple drone surveillance with automation) found accuracy on the harder task fell over time, more so with unreliable automation, and people relied on the automation less as time went on. Keep it to: sustained monitoring of automation is effortful and can degrade over time, and unreliable automation makes it worse. Say the second study was a simulation with students.
do_not_use: Do not claim Wohleber found high workload or rising stress (workload was low, distress flat). Do not present Wohleber as proof that supervising AI coding agents causes errors; it is drones, students, 2 hr. Do not quote Warm et al. body text or numbers (only the abstract was read). Do not use second-hand claims (Hancock, Matthews 2014 '1 SD') without opening them. Do not call it a 'meta-analysis' or imply Warm 2008 reports new experiments.
